recto: Name the epidermal layers from deep to surface
verso: Stratum basale → spinosum → granulosum → lucidum (thick skin only) → corneum. Thin skin has {v:A_COUCHES_FINE} layers, thick skin {v:A_COUCHES_EPAISSE}.

recto: Does the epidermis have blood vessels?
verso: No: it is avascular and is nourished from the dermis. A scrape that bleeds has reached the dermis.

recto: Where are melanocytes and what do they make?
verso: In the stratum basale of the epidermis; they make melanin, which helps protect epidermal DNA from UV damage.
Pick up antigens entering damaged skin and alert the immune system (stratum spinosum).

recto: How does the skin cool the body?
verso: Evaporating sweat carries heat away; dermal arterioles dilate to shed heat (and constrict in the cold to keep it).

recto: How does the skin contribute to vitamin D?
verso: With UV light the epidermis turns a cholesterol derivative into vitamin D<sub>3</sub>; the liver and kidneys activate it; it helps absorb calcium and phosphorus.

recto: Where do pressure injuries form and how are they prevented?
verso: Where bone lies close to the skin (heels, hips, ankles, elbows, back). Keep skin clean and dry, reposition about every {v:A_REPOSITIONNEMENT_H} h, use pressure-relieving surfaces.
Osteoblasts form bone; osteoclasts resorb it; osteocytes are mature cells in the matrix.
Compact: osteons with a central canal and lamellae. Spongy: trabeculae along lines of stress, spaces with red marrow.

recto: How many bones in the adult skeleton?
verso: {v:A_OS_ADULTE}: {v:A_OS_AXIAL} axial + {v:A_OS_APPEND} appendicular.
Axial: skull (with ossicles), hyoid, vertebral column, thoracic cage. Appendicular: pectoral and pelvic girdles plus the limbs.
Synarthroses (immovable, e.g., sutures), amphiarthroses (slightly movable, cartilage), diarthroses (freely movable, synovial; most adult joints).
Hip, vertebrae, wrist. Usually silent until a fracture.
Skeletal: striated, voluntary, many nuclei. Cardiac: striated, involuntary, one nucleus. Smooth: not striated, involuntary, one nucleus.
Sheaths around the whole muscle, each fascicle, each fiber.

recto: Steps from nerve impulse to contraction
verso: ACh at the neuromuscular junction → action potential along membrane and T-tubules → Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin → tropomyosin moves → myosin binds actin and pulls.

recto: What is ATP needed for in contraction?
verso: For myosin to detach from actin and re-cock, and to pump Ca²⁺ back. Without ATP cross-bridges lock (rigor mortis).
The sarcomere. Actin and myosin filaments keep their length and slide.

recto: Share of body heat from muscle contraction
verso: Nearly {v:A_CHALEUR_MUSCLE}%.

recto: Myasthenia gravis: mechanism and key sign
verso: Autoimmune: antibodies disrupt transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Weakness worsens with activity, improves with rest; drooping eyelids and double vision often first.
Dendrites carry impulses toward the cell body; the single axon carries them away.
Schwann cells in the PNS, oligodendrocytes in the CNS.

recto: Number of cranial and spinal nerve pairs
verso: {v:A_NERFS_CRANIENS} cranial; {v:A_NERFS_SPINAUX} spinal ({v:A_NS_C} C, {v:A_NS_T} T, {v:A_NS_L} L, {v:A_NS_S} S, {v:A_NS_CO} Co).
Dura mater, arachnoid (CSF in the subarachnoid space beneath it), pia mater.

recto: Resting potential and threshold of a typical neuron
verso: About {v:A_RMP} mV at rest; threshold about {v:A_SEUIL} mV.

recto: Ion movements of the action potential
verso: Depolarization: Na⁺ enters. Repolarization: K⁺ leaves. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump (ATP) restores the gradients.

recto: Functions of the four main cerebral lobes
verso: Frontal: motor, planning, Broca's area (speech production). Parietal: touch and body sense. Temporal: hearing, long-term memory. Occipital: vision.

recto: Which sense is not relayed by the thalamus?
verso: Smell (olfaction).
Sympathetic: thoracolumbar (fight or flight). Parasympathetic: craniosacral, including the vagus nerve (rest and digest).
Sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami.
Rods: dim light. Cones (three kinds): color. Fovea: sharpest vision; optic disc: blind spot.

recto: What detects rotation of the head?
verso: The semicircular canals (utricle and saccule: head position and linear acceleration).
Sudden one-sided numbness or weakness of face, arm or leg; confusion or trouble speaking; vision loss; trouble walking; sudden severe headache. Call 911 right away.

recto: Where are ADH and oxytocin made and released?
verso: Made in the hypothalamus; stored and released by the posterior pituitary.
GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin.
PTH raises blood Ca²⁺ (main regulator); calcitonin lowers it.
Insulin (beta cells) lowers blood glucose; glucagon (alpha cells) raises it.
Cortex: steroids (aldosterone, cortisol, small amounts of sex hormones). Medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine on sympathetic stimulation.
Steroids bind receptors inside the cell (slower, via protein synthesis); protein hormones bind surface receptors (faster).
